messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Community Organizer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 49

He is 63, a man from Oceania, divorced for many years, and he spends most of his time as a community organizer, the kind of person people know by voice before they know by name. Before the accident, he is the one setting up chairs before neighborhood meetings, calling elders to make sure they have rides, standing in front of church halls and school gyms with a clipboard under his arm and a joke ready. He likes being useful. He likes movement, noise, and the feeling that he can bring people together.

The accident happens on a wet afternoon three years ago, after a long day of visiting families about a housing petition. He is driving back along a coastal road he has taken for decades. He remembers the rain first—hard, slanting, sudden enough to blur the windshield even with the wipers working fast. Then he remembers a truck ahead of him braking, the red lights smearing in the rain, and the strange slow-motion second when his tires stop listening to him. The car skids. He feels the wheel jerk in his hands. There is the sound of metal folding, glass bursting inward, and then the car tipping just enough that he thinks, with complete certainty, This is how I die.

He is trapped for what he later learns is less than twenty minutes, though in his mind it stretches into something endless. He smells petrol. He cannot get his left leg free. Rain leaks through the broken window and runs down his neck. He hears other voices outside, far away and urgent, but he cannot answer at first because his jaw is shaking so hard. More than the pain, what stays with him is the helplessness. He is a man used to stepping in, solving problems, helping others. In that crushed car he can do nothing except wait and listen for the possibility of fire.

His body heals faster than the rest of him. He returns home with bruised ribs, a leg injury, and instructions to rest. Friends from the community bring soup, fruit, and stories from meetings he has missed. He smiles for them. He says he is lucky. He says others have had worse. At night he lies in bed and sees the red brake lights again, vivid as if projected onto the dark ceiling. Sometimes he wakes with his heart hammering, clawing at the sheets before he fully understands where he is. Rain becomes intolerable. During storms he checks the windows repeatedly, paces from room to room, and feels a pressure in his chest he cannot reason with.

When he first tries to drive again, he makes it only a few blocks before a bus hisses to a stop beside him and he jerks so hard at the sound that he nearly mounts the curb. After that he starts arranging rides, telling people his leg still bothers him. In truth, he cannot bear intersections, brake lights, or the moment a car in front slows unexpectedly. He studies every road for exits. If someone else is driving, he presses his foot into the floorboard as if he has a brake there too. He keeps scanning, never settling. By the time he reaches a destination, he is already tired.

His work changes in ways he does not immediately admit. He still attends community meetings, but now he chooses a chair near the back or close to the door. If a room gets too crowded or loud, he feels heat rising under his collar and slips outside for air without explanation. People notice he startles more easily. A dropped microphone, a slammed door, even a stack of plastic chairs falling in the hall can leave him rigid and silent for several moments. He laughs it off afterward, but inside he feels embarrassed and angry, as if his body has become disloyal.

He used to be known for remembering everyone’s troubles and making space for them. Now he finds himself losing the thread in conversations. When residents speak to him about evictions, water access, youth programs, he wants to listen the way he always has, but his concentration frays. On bad days he hears only fragments because part of him is elsewhere, back in the car, counting seconds and waiting to burn. He keeps busy because busyness feels safer than stillness, yet by evening he is worn down and irritable. Small frustrations—misplaced paperwork, a late phone call, a printer jamming—can set him off. Then comes guilt, heavy and familiar. He tells himself he should be stronger by now.

His divorce was years before the accident, but since it he feels the aloneness of his house more sharply. He has adult children who call and visit, and he gives them edited versions of how he is doing. He does not want them to think he is becoming fragile. He sleeps on the sofa some nights because the bedroom feels too enclosed. He avoids the coastal road completely, even when it means doubling his travel time for work. During heavy rain he cancels plans and tells people there are scheduling issues.

What troubles him most is that the world no longer feels ordinary. He moves through it as if danger sits just beneath the surface of routine things. A commute, a storm, the squeal of brakes outside a meeting hall—any of it can pull him backward in an instant. He still shows up for his community, still carries the clipboard, still calls elders to make sure they have rides. But he does these things while watching every exit, listening for impact, and wondering why a part of him remains on that road, in the rain, waiting to be cut free.
